rc-literary.q: 'The lonely lighthouse kept its watch all night.' The device used is:
rc-literary.explain: A lighthouse 'keeping watch' is a human action given to a thing — personification.

rc-literary.q: 'Her smile was sunshine after a week of rain.' This is a:
rc-literary.explain: It calls the smile 'sunshine' directly, with no 'like/as' — metaphor.

rc-literary.q: 'O Wind, tell me where the summer goes.' The poet is using:
rc-literary.explain: Addressing the wind as if it could answer is apostrophe.

rc-literary.q: 'The silence in the hall was deafening.' This figure of speech is:
rc-literary.explain: 'Deafening silence' pairs two opposite ideas — oxymoron.

rc-literary.q: Best first step when a poem question asks what a line 'means':
opts: Answer from the options at once
Re-read the line in its full sentence and paraphrase it plainly
rc-literary.explain: Figurative lines need to be read in context and put into plain words before matching an option.

rc-factual.q: A passage argues that urban tree cover lowers summer temperatures but is expensive to maintain. Which statement is best supported?
opts: Cities should remove trees to cut costs
Tree cover has both a clear benefit and a real cost
Maintenance is never worth the expense
rc-factual.explain: The passage gives one benefit and one cost — the balanced option matches; the others are too strong or contradict it.

rc-factual.q: A writer says a technology is 'promising but unproven at scale'. The writer's attitude is best described as:
rc-factual.explain: 'Promising' is positive; 'unproven at scale' holds back full endorsement — cautious optimism.

rc-factual.q: The passage states: 'Rainwater harvesting cut the village's tanker dependence by half within two years.' Which is a fact from the passage?
opts: Tanker dependence fell by about 50% in two years
The village still relies fully on tankers
rc-factual.explain: 'By half' = about 50%; 'within two years' is stated. The other options misstate the figure or timeline.

rc-factual.q: Which option would most weaken an argument that 'reading fiction improves empathy'?
opts: A study finds fiction readers score higher on empathy tests
Empathy and fiction-reading both simply rise with education level
rc-factual.explain: If a third factor (education) drives both, the fiction→empathy link may not be causal — that weakens it.

rc-factual.q: A main-idea question offers four options. Three restate single sentences from the passage; one covers the whole passage. The correct answer is usually:
opts: The option that covers the whole passage
rc-factual.explain: Main idea must span the passage, not paraphrase one detail.

rc-narrative.q: 'He said nothing, but the next morning my bicycle stood mended by the gate.' What does this suggest about the man?
opts: He showed care through action rather than words
rc-narrative.explain: The mended bicycle is a wordless act of care — shown, not stated.

rc-narrative.q: In a narrative, a character's feelings are usually revealed through:
opts: A direct statement of the moral
rc-narrative.explain: Narrative shows character indirectly through behaviour and speech.

rc-narrative.q: 'By the time the train pulled out, I had stopped waving.' What is the sequence?
opts: Waving stopped, then the train left
The train left, then waving started
The train left before it arrived
rc-narrative.explain: 'Had stopped' (past perfect) is the earlier event: waving ended, then the train departed.

rc-narrative.q: A narrative passage ends: 'I never took the short cut again.' This most likely signals:
opts: A lasting change caused by what happened
rc-narrative.explain: A closing line like this marks the narrator's changed behaviour — the point of the story.

rc-narrative.q: Which is the safest way to answer a 'why did the character do X' question?
opts: Use the reason given or clearly implied in the passage
rc-narrative.explain: Narrative answers come from the text's own cause-and-effect.

Reading Comprehension — hacks, shortcuts & reminders

Where the marks are

≈13 of 50 questions. Factual/expository ≈10 · Narrative ≈2 · Literary/poem ≈1. Passages are capped at 300 words and come in three tagged types: Factual, Narrative, Literary. Almost every question is answerable straight from the text — RC is a finding game, not a thinking game.

The 3-pass method

  1. Glance at the questions first (10–15 sec) — note what you're hunting for: a definition, a reason, a name, the main idea, an EXCEPT.
  2. Read the passage once at a steady pace. Lightly mark: the topic sentence of each paragraph, any name/date/number, and any strong opinion word (however, unfortunately, remarkably, must).
  3. Answer question by question, from the text. For each, put your finger on the exact line that proves the answer before you commit.

Time budget

≈72 sec per question overall. For a 5-question passage aim for ~5 min total — about 2 min reading, 3 min answering. If a passage is dense, take the 2–3 easy factual questions and move on; don't burn 8 minutes chasing one inference.

Question-type playbook

TypeHow to attack it
Main idea / best titleThe answer covers the whole passage. Reject options that are true but only about one paragraph, and options that are broader than the passage.
Stated detail ("according to the passage")Locate the line. The correct option is a paraphrase — same meaning, different words. An option that copies passage words is often the trap.
Inference ("it can be concluded", "the passage implies")Stay one small step from the text. If you need outside knowledge or a chain of assumptions, it's wrong. The safest inference is the least dramatic one.
Vocabulary-in-context ("the word X here means")Ignore the dictionary meaning you know. Substitute each option into the sentence; keep the one that doesn't change the meaning.
Tone / attitudeMatch to signal words. Most CUET factual passages are neutral, informative or mildly critical — rarely "angry", "sarcastic" or "pessimistic". Narrative tone is usually nostalgic, warm, reflective.
Purpose ("the author's main purpose is to")Pick the verb: to describe / explain / argue / persuade / narrate. Match it to how the passage actually reads.
EXCEPT / NOT / LEASTFlip it: tick the three options the passage does support; the leftover is the answer. Cross out the word EXCEPT so you don't forget.
"The author would agree with"Only what follows from the passage's own claims. A statement can be reasonable and still not be something this author said.
Structure ("the passage is organised as")Name the shape: problem→solution · claim→evidence · general→specific · chronological · compare–contrast.

Kill an option if it is…

  • Too absolute — always, never, only, all, none, must, impossible — in a hedged academic passage.
  • Half-right — one clause matches the passage, the other doesn't. A partly-wrong option is fully wrong.
  • Outside the passage — true in real life, but never stated here.
  • Right idea, wrong scope — a supporting detail offered as the main idea, or a sweeping claim where the passage was cautious.
  • Distorted — uses the passage's keywords but reverses or exaggerates the relationship.
  • Opposite — reads well but says the reverse of the text (watch not, no, un-, fails to).

Reminders while solving

  • Answer from the passage, not from what you believe. Your opinion is not evidence.
  • Two options look right? One will have a word that's slightly too strong or slightly off-scope. Find that word.
  • Don't re-read the whole passage for every question — you already mapped where things are.
  • A "vocabulary meaning" question inside RC is a free vocabulary mark — treat it as one.
  • If truly stuck between two, pick the milder, more general one and move on — don't lose 3 minutes.
  • Never leave an RC question blank unless you can't remove even one option (−1 rule).

By passage type

FactualFollow the argument's spine: claim → evidence → conclusion. Expect detail, inference and tone questions. Read for structure, not every word.
NarrativeTrack sequence, cause, and the narrator's feeling. The "point" is usually a small realisation or change at the end. Answers are understated — reject the most dramatic option.
Literary / poemRead the whole thing once for situation and mood. Re-read the referenced line in its full sentence; figurative lines rarely work word-by-word. Paraphrase in plain words before looking at options.

Figures of speech (for the literary question)

simile — like / as metaphor — direct ("he is a lion") personification — a thing acts human alliteration — repeated initial sound hyperbole — exaggeration oxymoron — opposite words together apostrophe — addressing the absent ("O Death!") onomatopoeia — the word sounds like its meaning transferred epithet — "a sleepless night" rhetorical question — asked for effect

Quick tests: like/as → simile. A thing performing a human action → personification (before metaphor). Two contradictory words side by side → oxymoron.

One-minute revision

Questions first · read once, mark structure · answer from the line, not from memory · correct = paraphrase · inference = one small step · EXCEPT = tick the other three · kill absolute / half-right / out-of-passage options · milder option wins a 50-50 · never blank unless you can't cut one option.
